title: Laid-Off H-1B Workers Face Tougher Scrutiny as Immigration Officials Crack Down on Backup Visa Routes
excerpt: With over 114,000 tech jobs cut in 2026, Indian visa holders are finding it harder to switch to visitor status while job hunting, as USCIS issues more denials and requests for evidence.
body:
• More than 114,000 tech workers have been laid off across nearly 150 companies in 2026, with Indian H-1B holders — the largest national group among visa workers — disproportionately affected.
  • Immigration attorneys report a significant spike in Requests for Evidence and Notices of Intent to Deny on B-1/B-2 change-of-status applications filed by laid-off H-1B workers.
  • The 60-day grace period after termination has become harder to navigate as hiring slows and AI-driven restructuring makes companies more cautious about new sponsorships.
  • A proposed $100,000 H-1B application fee, temporarily stayed by a court, has further shaken employer and worker confidence.

Indian technology professionals on H-1B visas are facing an increasingly hostile environment after layoffs eliminated more than 114,000 jobs across nearly 150 tech companies in 2026. The traditional safety nets — switching to visitor status while job hunting, or finding a new sponsor within the 60-day grace period — are fraying under tighter immigration enforcement.

The 60-Day Clock

Under USCIS rules, laid-off H-1B workers have a discretionary 60-day window from their last working day to find a new sponsoring employer, switch visa categories, or prepare to leave the country. That deadline, always tight, has become brutal in the current market.

Companies including Meta, Amazon, Oracle, LinkedIn, and Cisco have cut staff as artificial intelligence reshapes hiring and job design. Meta alone eliminated 8,000 positions — about 10 percent of its global workforce — in May. Indians accounted for 283,772 of 406,348 approved H-1B petitions in fiscal year 2025, according to USCIS data, making them by far the most exposed group.

"Meta alone eliminated 8,000 positions — about 10 percent of its global workforce — in May."

"Meta alone eliminated 8,000 positions — about 10 percent of its global workforce — in May."

Backup Routes Are Narrowing

Workers who traditionally switched to B-1 or B-2 visitor status as a stopgap, filing Form I-539 to extend their stay for up to six months while searching for new sponsorship, now face much closer scrutiny. US-based immigration attorney Rajiv Khanna told the Economic Times that his team is seeing a significant spike in Requests for Evidence and Notices of Intent to Deny on change-of-status applications — at a scale he described as beyond anything in his career.

"Families are now dealing with mortgage payments, apartment leases, children in schools, and uncertain immigration timelines all at once, with only 60 days to resolve it."

— Rajiv Khanna, US immigration attorney

Some workers are exploring F-1 student visas, O-1 extraordinary ability visas, and L-1 intra-company transfer routes. Canada's Express Entry and Global Talent Stream programs are attracting growing interest as alternative destinations.

The Double Shock

For many families, a layoff triggers what immigration experts call a "double shock." Income stops at the same moment that legal status becomes uncertain, and dependent spouses on H-4 visas often cannot replace lost earnings by entering the labor market. H-4 work authorization generally depends on the H-1B spouse having an approved I-140, the first step in the green card process.

The stakes are compounded for those who spent years in the green card backlog. Many have US-born children, home loans, and lives built around an immigration system that ties legal status directly to employment. A Blind poll cited in media reports suggested nearly half of Indian professionals in the US would consider returning to India if they lost their jobs.

Policy Headwinds

A Trump administration proposal to raise the H-1B application fee to $100,000 has been temporarily stayed by a court of appeals, but the threat has chilled employer willingness to sponsor new workers. Since September 2025, onshore movement from India to the US has been largely frozen, with Indian IT companies sending H-1B holders primarily for pending renewals.

The combination of AI-driven layoffs, tighter enforcement, and policy uncertainty has accelerated reverse migration. India's growing technology sector — with its expanding global capability centers, startup ecosystem, and remote work opportunities — is drawing professionals back to Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, and other tech hubs.

What's Next

The current wave differs from earlier downturns because companies are not simply trimming payroll. They are reorganizing entire functions around AI tools and automated systems, a structural shift that may permanently reduce demand for the entry-to-mid-level IT roles where Indian H-1B workers have long concentrated. For the thousands navigating the 60-day clock right now, the question is no longer just about finding a job — it is about whether the system they built their lives around still works.
